What these statuses mean

Every staged pallet waits for a truck. A truck has to be booked 2 to 8 hours before it reaches the gate, so the coordinator decides when to book and with which carrier: book early and the trailer may leave part-empty; wait for a full load and the oldest pallets age toward the customer's deadline. That trade-off is the coordinators' daily decision.

  • Small FCs: about 20 lower-volume Amazon FCs ("second-tier zones"). Each gets too few pallets for its own door, so they share 4 doors and often flip into a bigger FC.
  • Deadline close: an unbooked pallet is due at Amazon within 36 h.
  • Full load unbooked: enough unbooked pallets to fill a trailer.
  • Watch: an unbooked pallet is due within 60 h.
  • Truck at 07:45: booked and on its way.
  • Loading: a truck is at the door.
  • Filling: pallets are accumulating toward a full trailer.

Placeholders: the hours, pallet counts and lead times above are our assumptions for this synthetic day. The real values come from the warehouse's data. A stand-in rule books trucks here; in the OpEra version these are the moments where the plan books ahead from the prep forecast.

Data & assumptions

These two days are synthetic, built to look like a typical Amazon prep and cross-dock 3PL. Every number is an assumption, tagged by where the real value should come from. With your feed (pallet state changes, manifests, appointments), the timing, trucks and costs become your real ones; the movement of people and pallet jacks on the floor stays illustrative. Codes like ATL6 or RDU1 are Amazon fulfillment centers, named after the nearest airport plus a number; which FCs and their distances are illustrative here. The baseline's trucks come from a stand-in coordinator rule; OpEra's come from its planning model, on the same inputs.
